question: Ari controls [Bludgeon Brawl] and [Soldevi Digger]. They cast [Titania's Song]. Once it resolves, what are the characteristics of Soldevi Digger?
answer:
Soldevi Digger ends up as a colorless 2/2 artifact creature — Equipment with no abilities at all.

How the layers get there (CR 613.1a, 613.6, 613.7 — same timestamp order in each layer, no dependency applies):

- Layer 4 (types/subtypes): Bludgeon Brawl has the earlier timestamp, so it applies first and makes Soldevi Digger an Equipment (it qualified: at that point it was a noncreature, non-Equipment artifact). Then Titania's Song makes it an artifact creature. Result: Artifact Creature — Equipment.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Bludgeon Brawl first grants "equip {2}" and "Equipped creature gets +2/+0" (X = Soldevi Digger's mana value, which is 2 — that's {2} generic to equip). Then Titania's Song, with the later timestamp, removes all abilities — including Soldevi Digger's printed "{2}: Put the top card of your graveyard on the bottom of your library" and the two abilities Bludgeon Brawl just granted. Result: no abilities.
- Layer 7b: Titania's Song sets power and toughness each equal to mana value, so 2/2. Note the mana value used is still 2 ({2} generic on the printed card); Bludgeon Brawl doesn't change mana cost.
- Color: nothing changes it, so Soldevi Digger stays colorless (CR 105.2 — no colored mana symbols in its cost, no color indicator or color-defining ability).

Key point about CR 613.6: once Bludgeon Brawl's effect starts applying in layer 4, it keeps applying to Soldevi Digger in layer 6 even though by then Soldevi Digger is a creature and an Equipment — but its granted abilities are stripped anyway because Titania's Song's ability-removal has the later timestamp.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Bludgeon Brawl was already on the battlefield before Titania's Song resolved (as stated). If instead Titania's Song had the earlier timestamp, Bludgeon Brawl would then no longer apply — Soldevi Digger would be a creature, and Bludgeon Brawl only affects noncreature artifacts — so it would be a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities and no Equipment subtype. Also, if Titania's Song later leaves the battlefield, its own text says the effect continues until end of turn.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; both cards affect artifacts regardless of controller, and the provided rules contain nothing player-count-specific here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: It's a 2/2 artifact creature with no abilities. Applying Titania's Song would cause Bludgeon Brawl to no longer apply (since Soldevi Digger would be a creature). However, applying Bludgeon Brawl would not change how Titania's Song's effect is applied, so Bludgeon Brawl is dependent on Titania's Song. Titania's Song applies first, and then Bludgeon Brawl won't affect Soldevi Digger since it's a creature.

question: Avery manifests the top card of their library with [Soul Summons]. Then, they mutate [Trumpeting Gnarr] targeting the manifested creature. What are the characteristics of the resulting creature if Avery chooses to put the manifested creature on top?
answer:
The result is a single face-down mutated permanent that is a 2/2 colorless creature with no name, no card types beyond creature, no mana cost, and no printed characteristics of its own — those come from the topmost component, the manifested card, which is face down (110.5, 702.140e, 730.2a). Underneath it is Trumpeting Gnarr.

Details:

1. Legality of the target: Trumpeting Gnarr's mutate ability requires a non-Human creature with the same owner (702.140a). A face-down manifested creature has no creature types at all, so it isn't a Human and is a legal target, assuming Avery owns it.

2. Merging: as the mutating creature spell Trumpeting Gnarr resolves with a legal target, it doesn't enter the battlefield separately; it merges with the manifested creature to form one object represented by both cards, and Avery chooses top or bottom (702.140c, 608.3d, 730.1, 730.2a). Avery puts the manifested card on top, so Trumpeting Gnarr is the bottom component.

3. Characteristics: a merged/mutated permanent has the characteristics of its topmost component (730.2a), and "its other characteristics are derived from the topmost card or token" (702.140e). Because the top component is face down, the permanent stays a 2/2 colorless nameless creature with no mana cost — Trumpeting Gnarr's name, 3/3 body, Beast type, and {1}{G}{U} mana cost do not apply. This is a copiable effect applied in layer 1a (613.2, 613.2a).

4. Abilities: a mutated permanent has all abilities of each card representing it (702.140e), so it does have Trumpeting Gnarr's abilities — mutate {3}{G/U}{G/U} and "Whenever this creature mutates, create a 3/3 green Beast creature token" — even though it looks like a plain face-down 2/2. (Compare 707.3, where a face-down permanent that merely copies something keeps no abilities; here rule 702.140e specifically grants the abilities of every component.)

5. Trigger now: the merge is a mutate event, so the Trumpeting Gnarr trigger triggers and Avery creates one 3/3 green Beast creature token (702.140d).

6. Turning it face up: the top card is the manifested card, so the permanent can be turned face up for that card's mana cost if it's a creature card; doing so would make its characteristics those of that card (plus it would still keep the abilities of both components under 702.140e).

Assumption on ordering: I'm assuming Soul Summons fully resolved and the manifest was already on the battlefield before Trumpeting Gnarr was cast for its mutate cost, as stated. If Trumpeting Gnarr had instead been cast targeting some other creature, none of the above about the manifest would apply.

Player count makes no difference here — the interaction is entirely between Avery's own permanents, so it plays out identically in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: It is a 2/2 colorless face-down creature with no abilities. It is face-down because the topmost object is face-down, and this status defines its characteristics. This notably means that Trumpeting Gnarr's triggered ability won't trigger.

question: Nico controls [Urza's Saga] with two lore counters on it. Alexzander uses [Jinx] to change its land type. What happens?
answer:
Urza's Saga becomes (say) a Mountain, loses its chapter abilities, and — per the card's own ruling — is immediately sacrificed as a state-based action. Nico keeps nothing from it except whatever abilities other effects had already granted it (which disappear with the permanent).

Why:

1. Jinx sets the land's subtype to a basic land type. Under rule [305.7], setting a land's subtype means the land loses its old land type (Urza's Saga) and loses all abilities generated from its rules text and old land types, gaining the basic type's mana ability instead. So the three chapter abilities (I, II, III) — which are keyword abilities printed in its text box, rule [107.15a] / [714.2b] — are gone.
2. Jinx changes only land subtypes. It doesn't change card types or supertypes ([305.7], [205.4b]), so the permanent is still an enchantment with the enchantment subtype Saga, and it still has its two lore counters.
3. [Urza's Saga ruling #1] directly covers this: if Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, it is immediately sacrificed. That ruling is authoritative for this interaction.
   Note the tension worth knowing: the current wording of the state-based action, rules [704.5s] and [714.4], only sacrifices "a Saga permanent with one or more chapter abilities" whose lore counters meet or exceed its final chapter number. Read strictly, a Saga with zero chapter abilities has no final chapter number and wouldn't be sacrificed. Follow the card ruling as given here; at a sanctioned event confirm with a judge which wording applies.
4. Abilities granted by other effects are not removed by [305.7]. So the "{T}: Add {C}" and the "{2}, {T}: Create a 0/0 Construct" abilities Urza's Saga gained from its own resolved chapter I and II triggers ([Urza's Saga ruling #5]) technically survive the type change — but only until the sacrifice, which happens immediately as a state-based action before anyone gets priority. If Nico had priority in response to Jinx, activating those abilities first is the way to get value; after Jinx resolves it's too late.

Chapter III never triggers, since no lore counter is added by Jinx and the Saga is gone before Nico's next precombat main phase turn-based action ([505.4], [703.4f], [714.3c]).

Player count doesn't matter here: this works identically at a two-player table and in multiplayer, since Jinx targets a single land and the sacrifice is performed by that permanent's controller, Nico.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
In layer 4, Urza's Saga will have its land type overwritten as well as lose all of its chapter abilities. It will gain the abilities to tap for {C} and to create Construct tokens in layer 6, as those abilities are granted by a continuous effect that was generated when the previous chapter abilities resolved..

Since Urza's Saga no longer has any chapter abilities, it will remain at 2 lore counters and will not receive any more in future turns. It is not sacrificed.

question: Natalie controls [High Fae Trickster]. Allen activates the crew ability of [Capenna Express]. Before it resolves Natalie casts [One with the Stars] targeting Capenna Express. What happens when the crew ability resolves?
answer:
Natalie can't cast One with the Stars targeting Capenna Express at that moment — the crew ability is still on the stack, so Capenna Express is still just a noncreature artifact Vehicle and is not a legal target for an Aura that reads "Enchant creature or enchantment." The attempted cast is illegal and is rewound; Allen's crew ability then resolves normally and Capenna Express becomes an artifact creature (a 6/6) until end of turn.

Details:
- Crew is an activated ability: "Tap any number of other untapped creatures you control with total power N or greater: This permanent becomes an artifact creature until end of turn" [702.122a]. The creatures are tapped as a cost when Allen activates it; the type change happens only on resolution. Until then Capenna Express has no power or toughness and isn't a creature [208.3a].
- Because Capenna Express is neither a creature nor an enchantment while the crew ability is on the stack, it can't be chosen as the target of One with the Stars. Target legality is checked both on casting and again on resolution [608.2b].
- High Fae Trickster's "You may cast spells as though they had flash" lets Natalie cast One with the Stars at instant speed, but it doesn't change what the Aura can legally enchant.
- If instead Natalie waits until after the crew ability resolves, Capenna Express is then an artifact creature and is a legal target. One with the Stars would make it an enchantment that loses all other card types, and per One with the Stars ruling #1 it stays an enchantment even after the crew effect would have expired at end of turn.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Capenna Express will become an artifact creature as normal. One with the Stars and Capenna Express's abilities both apply in layer 4 and attempt to change its type. Capenna Express's ability will have the newer timestamp, and it resolved most recently. ([613.7], [613.7b], [702.122a])

question: Niko controls [Urza's Saga] on chapter 2. Ainsley casts [Magus of the Moon]. What happens to Urza's Saga?
answer:
Urza's Saga is put into Niko's graveyard immediately — Niko sacrifices it as a state-based action.

Why: Magus of the Moon says "Nonbasic lands are Mountains." That makes Urza's Saga a Mountain, which sets its land subtype to Mountain and removes its rules text (leaving "{T}: Add {R}"), so it loses its chapter I, II, and III abilities. It does not, however, lose the enchantment subtype Saga (Magus of the Moon changes land types only, and per [Magus of the Moon ruling #1] it doesn't touch names or supertypes either).

So Urza's Saga is still a Saga permanent, but it now has no chapter abilities. Rule [704.5s]/[714.4] only sacrifices a Saga that has one or more chapter abilities and enough lore counters — but [Urza's Saga ruling #1] states this case explicitly: "If Urza's Saga loses all of its chapter abilities but is still a Saga, perhaps due to a card like Blood Moon, it will immediately be sacrificed." Magus of the Moon has the same effect as Blood Moon here, so Urza's Saga is sacrificed the next time state-based actions are checked, regardless of it sitting on chapter 2.

Timing note: Magus of the Moon must resolve first. While Ainsley's Magus of the Moon is still on the stack, Urza's Saga is unaffected — Niko can still activate its chapter II Construct-making ability (and hold priority to do so) before Magus of the Moon resolves. Any Construct token already created stays; only Urza's Saga itself is sacrificed. Niko also loses the chapter III search, since chapter III will never trigger.

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table: Magus of the Moon affects every nonbasic land in play, so every player's Urza's Saga (and any similar Saga land) is sacrificed by its own controller.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
It becomes an Enchantment Land - Saga Mountain with an ability to tap for {R}, an ability to tap for {1}, an ability to create Constructs, and no other abilities.

Since it no longer has any chapter abilities, it will remain at 2 lore counters and will not receive any more in future turns. It is not sacrificed.

question: Ahmad controls [Conspiracy] (naming "Ferret"), [Kormus Bell], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth], and a [Vastwood Zendikon] enchanting Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth that entered the battlefield in that order. Is Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth a creature? If so, what are its creature types?
answer:
Yes — Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature, and its only creature type is Ferret. Its full type line ends up as "Legendary Land Creature — Swamp Ferret" (Swamp is a land type, Ferret the creature type), and it's a 6/4 green creature.

How it gets there, working through the type-changing effects in timestamp order:

1. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth's own ability makes each land a Swamp in addition to its other land types, including itself while it's on the battlefield ([Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #0], [Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth ruling #2]).
2. Kormus Bell then sees a Swamp: "All Swamps are 1/1 black creatures that are still lands," so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth becomes a land creature and keeps its land types and its Legendary supertype ([205.1b], [205.4b], [Kormus Bell ruling #0]).
3. Vastwood Zendikon makes the enchanted land a 6/4 green Elemental creature that's still a land ([Vastwood Zendikon ruling #5]). Since it's later than Kormus Bell, it sets the color to green and the power/toughness to 6/4.
4. Conspiracy, though it entered first, has to be applied after the others in the type-changing layer: it only affects creatures Ahmad controls, and whether Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is a creature at all is determined by Kormus Bell and Vastwood Zendikon. Applying Conspiracy last, it sets the creature type to the chosen type, Ferret, and the permanent loses all other creature types — so the Elemental type from Vastwood Zendikon is gone ([Conspiracy ruling #4]). Conspiracy can grant a creature type to animated lands that would otherwise have none ([Conspiracy ruling #1]).

Notes: Conspiracy changes only creature types, so the land type Swamp ([205.3c] — subtypes correlate to the card type they belong to) and the Legendary supertype ([205.4b]) both remain. Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth still has all its card types (land and creature) and satisfies anything that cares about either ([205.2b]). Conspiracy also doesn't rewrite creature-type words in card text ([Conspiracy ruling #0]).

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since all four permanents are Ahmad's.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: It is an Elemental Ferret creature. Conspiracy has the earliest timestamp, but it's dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, and waits to apply until after Vastwood Zendikon is applied. Kormus Bell is dependent on Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth, so Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is applied first, then Kormus Bell. At this point Conspiracy is no longer be dependent on Vastwood Zendikon, so Conspiracy is applied, and then Vastwood Zendikon. Since Vastwood Zendikon says that Urborg, Tomb of Yawgmoth is still a land, it retains its prior creature type of "Ferret" when it becomes an Elemental.

question: Aubree casts [Blood Moon]. Nikolas activates [Inkmoth Nexus]'s ability in response. What will Inkmoth Nexus look like after everything resolves? What will it look like next turn?
answer:
After everything resolves, Inkmoth Nexus is a 1/1 land artifact creature with the land type Mountain and exactly one ability: "{T}: Add {R}." It has no flying, no infect, no {T}: Add {C}, and no Phyrexian Blinkmoth land-type text — but it is still a 1/1 creature.

Why (CR 613.6 layer order; Inkmoth Nexus's ability resolved first, so it has the earlier timestamp, and Blood Moon's static effect starts applying when Blood Moon resolves, later):
- Layer 4 (type-changing, CR 613.1d): Inkmoth Nexus's ability makes it an artifact creature — Phyrexian Blinkmoth that's still a land. Then Blood Moon applies, changing its land subtype to Mountain (Blood Moon ruling #2). Blood Moon only changes land types and doesn't touch supertypes or the name (Blood Moon ruling #1), so Inkmoth Nexus remains a land artifact creature, just with Mountain in place of its other land types.
- Layer 6 (abilities): Inkmoth Nexus's ability grants flying and infect first; then Blood Moon, with the later timestamp, strips all of the land's abilities and grants "{T}: Add {R}" (Blood Moon ruling #2). Because Blood Moon applies after, the granted flying and infect are removed too, and the {T}: Add {C} and the {1} animation ability are gone.
- Layer 7b (setting P/T): the "becomes a 1/1" part of Inkmoth Nexus's ability still applies. Per CR 613.6, once an effect starts applying in one layer it keeps applying in every other applicable layer even though the ability generating it has been removed — so Inkmoth Nexus is 1/1 despite no longer having the ability that animated it.

Next turn: Inkmoth Nexus's animation was "until end of turn," so it wears off in the cleanup step. With Blood Moon still on the battlefield, next turn Inkmoth Nexus is simply a nonbasic land — Mountain with "{T}: Add {R}" and nothing else. Nikolas can no longer activate the {1} animation ability, because Blood Moon has removed it.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nikolas activated in response, so Inkmoth Nexus's ability resolved before Blood Moon. If instead Blood Moon had already resolved first, Nikolas couldn't activate the ability at all — Blood Moon would already have removed it.

Player count doesn't matter here; the provided rules on layers apply identically in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Inkmoth Nexus will be a 1/1 Artifact Land Creature - Mountain Blinkmoth with flying, infect, {T}: Add {R}, and no other abilities. Next turn it will be a Land - Mountain with {T}: Add {R} and no other abilities. Setting a land's subtype to a basic land type causes it to lose all other land types, as well as all abilities granted by its rules text, and gain the appropriate mana ability from its new land type. It will still keep abilities granted to it by other effects as those are gained in layer 6 while Blood Moon's type-changing effect applies in layer 4, so it will still have flying and infect. Removing the activated ability from Inkmoth Nexus does not affect the instance of the ability that has already resolved, so the effect will end as normal and Inkmoth Nexus will not be a creature next turn.

question: Alannah controls [Ore-Rich Stalactite], [Life and Limb], [March of the Machines], and [Xenograft] naming "Saproling", that entered the battlefield in that order. What is the Ore-Rich Stalactite?
answer:
Ore-Rich Stalactite ends up as a 1/1 green Saproling Forest artifact creature — an artifact land creature that also still has its own printed abilities.

How it gets there, layer by layer:

**Layer 4 (types/subtypes), applied in timestamp order:**
- March of the Machines makes each noncreature artifact an artifact creature, so Ore-Rich Stalactite becomes an artifact creature.
- Xenograft (naming Saproling) makes each creature you control that type in addition to its others, so Ore-Rich Stalactite is now a Saproling. (Xenograft depends on March of the Machines having made it a creature; the timestamp order given already applies them that way.)
- Life and Limb says all Forests and all Saprolings are 1/1 green Saproling creatures and Forest lands in addition to their other types. Since Ore-Rich Stalactite is now a Saproling, Life and Limb also makes it a Forest land. So its types are artifact land creature — Saproling Forest — the artifact/land combination described under Artifact Land, subject to the rules for both.

**Layer 5 (color):** Life and Limb makes it green (it was otherwise colorless as an artifact).

**Layer 7b (setting power/toughness):** March of the Machines sets it to its mana value, 2/2; Life and Limb sets it to 1/1. Life and Limb has the later timestamp, so the final result is 1/1. Note that per rule 613.6, March of the Machines keeps applying its power/toughness part to the same object even though that object is no longer a "noncreature artifact" by layer 7b — it's just overwritten by the later effect.

**Abilities:** Because it has the basic land type Forest, it has the intrinsic ability "{T}: Add {G}" (rule 305.6) — that's {G}, green mana, not the {R} from its own ability. It also keeps its printed "{T}: Add {R}. Spend this mana only to cast an instant or sorcery spell" and its Craft ability. Since it's now a creature, summoning sickness applies to tapping it for either mana ability unless it has been under Alannah's control since her most recent turn began.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
It's a 2/2 colorless Artifact Creature - Saproling.

In layer 4, Life and Limb's effect is not dependent on March of the Machines or Xenograft, so Life and Limb is applied first, then March of the Machines, then Xenograft. Since Life and Limb didn't apply to Ore-Rich Stalactite in layer 4, it doesn't apply to it in later layers either.

question: Autumn controls [Painter's Servant] naming "blue" and [Sword of Body and Mind]. Nico casts [Gift of Tusks] targeting the Painter's Servant. After it resolves, what happens if Autumn tries to equip Painter's Servant with Sword of Body and Mind?
answer:
The equip works, and Sword of Body and Mind stays attached.

Why: Gift of Tusks makes Painter's Servant lose all abilities and become a green Elephant with base power and toughness 3/3. Losing all abilities removes Painter's Servant's color-changing ability, so nothing is making other objects blue anymore [113.10]. (Even while that ability worked, Gift of Tusks' own color-setting effect would apply on top of it for Painter's Servant itself [Painter's Servant ruling #4].)

Equip {2} means "{2}: Attach this permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery" [702.6a]. Painter's Servant is still a creature Autumn controls, so it's a legal target, and Sword of Body and Mind can legally be attached to a creature [301.5c]. The {2} is two generic mana, payable with any color or with colorless mana.

On resolution, Sword of Body and Mind attaches (receiving a new timestamp) [701.3c] and grants +2/+2 and protection from green and from blue. Protection would make an Equipment fall off as a state-based action only if that Equipment itself has the stated quality [702.16d, 704.1]. Sword of Body and Mind is a colorless artifact — it is neither green nor blue, because Painter's Servant's ability is gone. So it stays on, and Painter's Servant is a 5/5 green Elephant with protection from green and from blue until end of turn.

Contrast: if Painter's Servant still had its ability naming blue, Sword of Body and Mind would be blue and would immediately become unattached as a state-based action while remaining on the battlefield [702.16d].

Timing note: this assumes Autumn activates equip after Gift of Tusks has fully resolved, as stated. If Autumn had already attached Sword of Body and Mind before Gift of Tusks resolved, the Sword would have been blue (from Painter's Servant) and would have fallen off as soon as protection from blue applied; after Gift of Tusks resolves it could then be re-equipped as described.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same with two players or more.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
It becomes equipped and then becomes unequipped.

Gift of Tusks makes Painter's Servant lose all abilities, but this happens after color-changing effects have applied, so all cards are still blue. Nothing prevents the Sword of Body and Mind from becoming attached to Painter's Servant. Once Sword of Body and Mind is equipped to the Painter's Servant, it has protection from blue (the effect removing its abilities is applied before the effect giving it protection from blue, and so can't be equipped by anything blue. It becomes unattached as a state-based action.

question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?
answer:
Duplicant is a 4/4 (and an Artifact Creature — Shapeshifter Zombie Elemental).

Why: Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's third ability says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Exile is neither hand nor library, so all three +1/+1 counters stay on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card in exile (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #5, ruling #1 — the ability works because Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had it in the zone it left, the battlefield). Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text overrides the general expectation that counters fall off on a zone change.

A +1/+1 counter on a creature card in a zone other than the battlefield still adds to that card's power and toughness ([122.1a]), and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2 confirms exactly this (a Skullbriar, the Walking Grave with one counter in the command zone is 2/2). So the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card is 1/1 base plus three counters = 4/4.

Duplicant's static ability then gives Duplicant "the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it," so Duplicant's base 2/4 is overwritten in layer 7b ([613.1g], [613.4a] for the layer-7 sublayer framework) with 4/4, and it gains Zombie and Elemental while staying a Shapeshifter. Duplicant ruling #0 notes Duplicant's base power/toughness change to the imprinted card's, and any counters or effects on Duplicant itself would still apply on top (there are none here).

Note the limit in Duplicant ruling #2: characteristic-defining abilities that define a * apply in exile, but abilities that add or subtract power/toughness don't. Counters are not such an ability — they're markers that modify the card's power and toughness directly ([122.1a]), so they do count.

One timing note: this assumes the counters were on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave when it was exiled. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had somehow lost its counter-retention ability before leaving the battlefield (e.g., an effect stripping its abilities, per Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1), the counters would vanish and Duplicant would be 1/1 instead.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of players; the same result holds in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Duplicant is a 1/1. Duplicant has a non-characteristic defining ability that sets its power and toughness. This is applied in layer 7b, at which point Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's power and toughness is still 1/1 because power and toughness changes from counters are not applied until layer 7c.

question: Nico controls [Thespian's Stage] that's currently a copy of [Temple of Triumph]. Alayna casts [Alpine Moon] and names "Temple of Triumph" as it resolves. Alayna then activates a second Thespian's Stage targeting Temple of Triumph. What does each Thespian's Stage look like?
answer:
Nico's Thespian's Stage is now a land named Temple of Triumph with no land types and exactly one ability, "{T}: Add one mana of any color" — it has lost the Thespian's Stage copy ability, so Nico can't re-copy anything with it. Alayna's second Thespian's Stage, once its ability resolves, is an untapped-or-tapped-as-it-already-was land that's a full copy of Temple of Triumph ("This land enters tapped," "When this land enters, scry 1," "{T}: Add {R} or {W}") plus the Thespian's Stage copy ability, and Alpine Moon does not touch it.

Why:

Nico's Stage — the copy effect from Thespian's Stage is applied in layer 1 (CR 613.1a, 613.2a), so its copiable values are those of Temple of Triumph, except it also keeps "{2}, {T}: This land becomes a copy of target land, except it has this ability" (CR 707.9a, and Thespian's Stage ruling #0: the copy has no duration and it loses the {T}: Add {C} ability). Its name is therefore "Temple of Triumph," so Alpine Moon's chosen name matches. Alpine Moon affects lands opponents of Alayna control, and Nico is such an opponent. Its type-changing part applies in layer 4 (removing land types — Temple of Triumph has none, and per Alpine Moon ruling #1 the land card type and any supertypes stay) and its ability part in layer 6: lose all abilities, then gain "{T}: Add one mana of any color." Because "lose all abilities" is applied before the grant within the same effect, the granted mana ability survives, but the copied Temple abilities and the Stage's own copy ability are gone. Nico's land is still tapped or untapped exactly as it was — becoming a copy never untaps it (Thespian's Stage ruling #2).

Alayna's Stage — Alpine Moon only hits lands Alayna's opponents control, so her own land is unaffected. When she copies "Temple of Triumph," she copies its copiable values: Alpine Moon is a type-changing/ability-changing continuous effect, not a copy effect, so those changes are not copied (CR 707.2, Thespian's Stage ruling #3). This is true whether she targets a real Temple of Triumph or Nico's Stage — copying Nico's Stage yields Nico's copiable values (Temple of Triumph + the Stage copy ability, per CR 707.3/707.9a), stripped of Alpine Moon's effect. No enters-the-battlefield effects apply, so "enters tapped" and the scry 1 do nothing now (Thespian's Stage ruling #1); it just sits there with those abilities as text, plus "{T}: Add {R} or {W}" and the copy ability.

One wrinkle worth naming: Alayna's Stage is now also named "Temple of Triumph," but Alpine Moon only affects lands Alayna's *opponents* control, so it stays untouched. In a multiplayer game the same logic scales: every land named Temple of Triumph controlled by any opponent of Alayna gets stripped and gains the any-color mana ability; lands Alayna controls never do.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Both Thespian's Stages are lands named "Temple of Triumph" and have "{T}: Add one mana of any color." and no other abilities. Because Thespian's Stage gains its ability as part of the copying process, the ability applies in the copy layer, which is earlier than the adding and removing abilities layer.

question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?
answer:
Yes — after the equip resolves, Wandering Ones has flying (and haste), and is a -5/1 creature.

Why: Fleetfeather Sandals and Tightening Coils both produce continuous effects in layer 6 (ability adding/removing), so they're ordered by timestamp [613.1f, 613.7a]. Neither depends on the other; the later one simply wins [613.9]. An Equipment receives a new timestamp each time it becomes attached to an object [613.7e], so re-activating Fleetfeather Sandals's Equip {2} and attaching it again to Wandering Ones gives its "Equipped creature has flying and haste" ability a timestamp later than Tightening Coils. Applying in order: Tightening Coils removes flying, then Fleetfeather Sandals grants flying and haste — so Wandering Ones ends up with flying. This matches Tightening Coils ruling #0: if an effect gives the enchanted creature flying after Tightening Coils became attached, the creature has flying.

Tightening Coils's -6/-0 applies in layer 7c regardless, so Wandering Ones is 1-6 = -5 power, 1 toughness (a negative power counts as 0 for dealing damage purposes). Multiple instances of flying would be redundant anyway [702.9c].

Note that Equip only works as a sorcery and can be activated even if Fleetfeather Sandals is already attached to that same creature; re-attaching it is what refreshes the timestamp [702.6d, 604.4]. Player count doesn't matter here — the same layer ordering applies in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Tightening Coils became attached before the equip activation, as stated. If instead Fleetfeather Sandals had been attached last before Tightening Coils and never re-equipped, Tightening Coils would have the later timestamp and Wandering Ones would not have flying.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: No. Tightening Coils has the most recent timestamp, so its effect is applied last. Activating Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability targeting Wandering Ones doesn't change its timestamp.

question: Ayla controls [Living Plane] and plays [Minas Tirith]. Does it enter tapped or untapped?
answer:
Minas Tirith enters untapped.

Why: Living Plane says "All lands are 1/1 creatures that are still lands," a continuous effect that already exists and applies to every land, including Minas Tirith. Minas Tirith's own "enters tapped unless you control a legendary creature" is a replacement effect that modifies how it enters the battlefield, so you check the characteristics of Minas Tirith as it would exist on the battlefield, taking into account continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it [614.12]. On the battlefield under Living Plane, Minas Tirith would be a legendary 1/1 creature land that Ayla controls, and the card says "a legendary creature," not "another legendary creature" — so it satisfies its own condition and enters untapped.

Two caveats worth flagging:

1. The Minas Tirith ruling that "the legendary creature must already be on the battlefield as the land enters; if it enters the battlefield at the same time, the land will enter tapped" is about a *separate* legendary creature entering simultaneously with Minas Tirith [Minas Tirith ruling #1]. It doesn't stop Living Plane's pre-existing effect from being applied to Minas Tirith itself under [614.12]. If Ayla instead had some other legendary creature entering at the same moment as Minas Tirith, that one would not count.

2. Being untapped doesn't mean Minas Tirith is immediately usable as a mana source in every sense: because Living Plane makes it a creature, it's subject to summoning sickness, so its {T} abilities ("{T}: Add {W}" and "{1}{W}, {T}: Draw a card") can't be activated and it can't attack unless Ayla has controlled it continuously since the beginning of her most recent turn [Living Plane ruling #2]. So the turn Ayla plays it, it sits untapped but can't tap for {W}.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Tapped. When applying an enters-the-battlefield replacement effect, the game considers the characteristics of the permanent as it would exist on the battlefield, so it sees that it would be a creature, but it doesn't consider the permanent to actually be on the battlefield yet. Effectively, a legendary creature is entering the battlefield.

question: Anderson controls [Quirion Explorer]. Nico controls [Crumbling Vestige]. If Anderson taps Quirion Explorer, what type(s) of mana can it produce?
answer:
Quirion Explorer produces no mana. Anderson can still tap it — the ability can be activated and it resolves — but it adds nothing to Anderson's mana pool.

Why: Quirion Explorer's ability adds "one mana of any color that a land an opponent controls could produce." The only land Nico controls is Crumbling Vestige, whose mana ability is "{T}: Add {C}." {C} is colorless mana, not a color — it is not {W}, {U}, {B}, {R}, or {G}, and it is not generic mana either. Since Crumbling Vestige could produce no *colored* mana, there is no legal color for Quirion Explorer's ability to add, so it produces nothing [106.7]. This is exactly the case covered by Quirion Explorer's own ruling: if the opponent only has lands that produce colorless or no mana, the ability can still be activated, it just won't produce any mana [Quirion Explorer ruling #1].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Crumbling Vestige is already on the battlefield and its "When this land enters, add one mana of any color" trigger has already resolved (or never was on the stack). If instead Crumbling Vestige has just entered and that triggered mana ability is still pending, there is a reasonable argument under 106.7 — which speaks of "any type of mana that an ability of that permanent would produce if the ability were to resolve at that time" — that the pending trigger makes any of the five colors available to Quirion Explorer. The rules text provided here doesn't cleanly settle whether a once-only enters-the-battlefield mana trigger counts for "could produce," so treat that narrow window as unresolved by the provided material; in every other case the answer is no mana.

Multiplayer note: Quirion Explorer says "a land an opponent controls," so at a table with more than two players you check the lands of *all* of Anderson's opponents, not just Nico's — if any other opponent controlled, say, a Forest, Quirion Explorer could add {G}. With only Anderson and Nico, Crumbling Vestige is the only land to check.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Any color. Quirion Explorer checks to see what mana Crumbling Vestige could produce if any of its abilities were to resolve at that time. That includes triggered abilities.

question: Andi controls [Karn Liberated], which has exiled an [Anvil of Bogardan]. They activate Karn Liberated's -14 ability, and restarts the game. How many cards will they draw during their first turn?
answer:
Direct answer: In a two-player game, Andi draws zero cards during their first turn. In a game with three or more players, Andi draws two cards (their normal draw for the turn plus Anvil of Bogardan's extra card) and then discards one.

Why:

1. Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game, and the player who controlled the restarting ability — Andi — is the starting player in the new game [727.1a]. Anvil of Bogardan, having been exiled with Karn Liberated by one of its first two abilities, stays in exile through the restart and is then put onto the battlefield under Andi's control after the pregame procedure but before the new game's first turn [Karn Liberated ruling #5, Karn Liberated ruling #7]. So Anvil of Bogardan is already on the battlefield when Andi's first turn begins, and it's treated as having been under Andi's control since the beginning of that turn [Karn Liberated ruling #3].

2. Two-player game: the player who plays first skips the draw step of their first turn [103.8a]. To skip a step is to proceed past it as though it didn't exist [500.11], and anything scheduled for a skipped step simply doesn't happen [614.10a]. Since Anvil of Bogardan's ability triggers "at the beginning of each player's draw step," and Andi has no first-turn draw step at all, the ability never triggers — no extra draw and no discard. Note this is different from Anvil of Bogardan ruling #1: that ruling covers the case where the draw *event* inside the resolving ability is replaced, in which case the discard still happens. Here the whole step, and therefore the trigger itself, never occurs. Total cards drawn on Andi's first turn: 0.

3. Three or more players: rule 103.8a's skipped draw step applies only "in a two-player game," so Andi does get a draw step on turn one. Andi draws their card for the turn, then Anvil of Bogardan's ability goes on the stack (it's put on the stack after the turn-based draw has already happened) [Anvil of Bogardan ruling #4], resolves, Andi draws an additional card and discards a card. Total drawn: 2, with one discard.

Not counted above: the seven-card opening hand (and any mulligans) is part of the new game's pregame procedure [727.1a], not a draw during Andi's first turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: 0. Their entire draw step is skipped. Andi will be the starting player in the new game. Because they is the starting player they'll skip their first draw step. Anvil of Bogardan triggers at the beginning of the draw step, but it doesn't get a chance to trigger if that step is skipped.

question: Amos controls [March of the Machines] and [Mycosynth Lattice] and casts [Lust for War] targeting their [Gilded Sentinel]. What will happen when Lust for War resolves?
answer:
Lust for War will resolve and enter the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel, but it will immediately fall off and go to Amos's graveyard — it never gets to do anything.

Step by step:

1. While Lust for War is still a spell on the stack, Mycosynth Lattice doesn't affect it. Mycosynth Lattice only makes permanents artifacts, and spells on the stack aren't permanents (Mycosynth Lattice ruling #2).
2. Gilded Sentinel is a legal object for Lust for War's "Enchant creature" ability, so Lust for War resolves and enters the battlefield attached to Gilded Sentinel ([303.4d]).
3. The instant Lust for War is on the battlefield, Mycosynth Lattice makes it an artifact in addition to being an enchantment — Aura. March of the Machines then sees a noncreature artifact and turns it into an artifact creature with power and toughness equal to its mana value. Lust for War's mana value is 3 ({2}{R}), so it becomes a 3/3 artifact creature that is still an enchantment — Aura (March of the Machines ruling #2).
4. An Aura that's also a creature can't enchant anything. The next time state-based actions are checked, Lust for War becomes unattached from Gilded Sentinel, and then as a second state-based action it's put into its owner's graveyard ([303.4d], Mycosynth Lattice ruling #4).

So Gilded Sentinel is never actually enchanted for any meaningful length of time: neither the "deals 3 damage when tapped" trigger nor the "attacks each combat if able" requirement will ever apply. Note that Lust for War dies because it's an Aura that's a creature, not because of a toughness problem — as a 3/3 it isn't destroyed for lethal damage or 0 toughness.

One timing note: this assumes Gilded Sentinel is still a legal target when Lust for War resolves. If Gilded Sentinel had left the battlefield or otherwise become an illegal target first, Lust for War would simply fail to resolve and be put into the graveyard as a countered spell instead — the same end zone, just for a different reason.

Player count doesn't matter here. Nothing in this interaction involves choosing an opponent or a defending player, so the result is identical in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Lust for War cannot legally enchant anything, so it will be put directly into its owners graveyard.

question: Aimee controls a manifested [Wayward Angel] and has 7 cards in their graveyard. Noah casts [Turn to Frog], targeting Wayward Angel. After that resolves, Aimee turns Wayward Angel face up. What are Wayward Angel's characteristics afterwards?
answer:
**Wayward Angel ends up as a face-up, black 4/4 Creature — Frog named Wayward Angel with flying, vigilance, trample, and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature," plus its Threshold ability.**

Why each characteristic comes out that way:

**Timestamps are the key.** Turn to Frog's continuous effect got its timestamp when Turn to Frog resolved [613.7b]. When Aimee then turns Wayward Angel face up, the permanent receives a *new* timestamp at that moment [613.7f]. Since effects within a layer are applied in timestamp order [613.3, 613.7], everything generated by Wayward Angel's own printed abilities is applied *after* Turn to Frog's effects.

- **Abilities (layer 6):** Turn to Frog's "loses all abilities" is applied in layer 6 [613.1f], but Wayward Angel's printed abilities now carry the later face-up timestamp, so they are applied after the removal and Wayward Angel has flying, vigilance, and the Threshold ability again [613.3, 613.7, 613.7f]. Compare Turn to Frog ruling: abilities that start applying after Turn to Frog are kept [Turn to Frog ruling #4].
- **Threshold is active:** Aimee has seven cards in their graveyard, so Threshold grants +3/+3, black, trample, and the upkeep sacrifice trigger.
- **Color (layer 5):** Turn to Frog makes it blue [613.1e]; Threshold's "is black" is applied later in the same layer, so Wayward Angel is black only — not blue, and not white-and-black [Wayward Angel ruling #1].
- **Creature type (layer 4):** Turn to Frog sets the creature type to Frog and removes other creature types; nothing later changes that, so it's a Frog, not an Angel Horror. It keeps other card types and supertypes it may have [Turn to Frog ruling #2].
- **Power/toughness:** Turn to Frog sets base power and toughness to 1/1 in layer 7b [Turn to Frog ruling #1], and Threshold's +3/+3 is a modification applied in layer 7c, which applies regardless of when it started [Turn to Frog ruling #3, 613.6]. 1/1 + 3/+3 = **4/4**.
- Because it's face up, it's no longer a 2/2 colorless nameless manifest — it's Wayward Angel with mana cost {4}{W}{W} (mana value 6), even though its current color is black.

**Timing assumption:** I'm reading the sequence exactly as stated — Turn to Frog fully resolved first, then Wayward Angel was turned face up. If instead Wayward Angel had been turned face up *before* Turn to Frog resolved, Turn to Frog would hold the later timestamp: it would strip flying, vigilance, and Threshold entirely, leaving a blue 1/1 Frog with no abilities (still named Wayward Angel).

**Player count:** none of this depends on the number of players — the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: It's a 4/4 black Frog with trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature", but no other abilities. Wayward Angel receives a new timestamp when it turns face up, so its ability is applied before Turn to Frog in each layer. Wayward Angel's last ability is removed by Turn to Frog in layer 6, but since it's already started to apply in layer 5 to change its color to black, it will continue doing so in later layers. Turn to Frog has the earlier timestamp, so it makes Wayward Angel blue before it becomes black in layer 5 and removes Wayward Angel's abilities in layer 6 before it gains trample and "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice a creature".

question: Amelia attacks with [Wildfire Eternal], which isn't blocked. As the trigger resolves, can they choose to suspend [Shivan Meteor]?
answer:
No. Amelia cannot suspend Shivan Meteor during the resolution of Wildfire Eternal's triggered ability. Exiling a card with suspend is a special action, and a player may take that special action only when they have priority — no player receives priority in the middle of a spell or ability resolving [116.2f, 608.2g, Shivan Meteor ruling #3].

Why: "Suspend N—[cost]" is a static ability of a card in hand that lets you pay the suspend cost and exile the card with N time counters on it; that action doesn't use the stack and isn't casting the card [702.62a, Shivan Meteor ruling #3, Shivan Meteor ruling #12]. Wildfire Eternal's trigger says "you may cast an instant or sorcery spell from your hand without paying its mana cost" — an effect that specifically instructs a player to cast a spell during resolution. That permission covers casting only; it does not grant priority or permission to take special actions [608.2g].

What Amelia can do instead: as Wildfire Eternal's trigger resolves (during the declare blockers step, before combat damage), Amelia may cast Shivan Meteor itself from hand for free, paying neither {3}{R}{R} nor the {1}{R}{R} suspend cost, choosing a target creature for its 13 damage at that time [Wildfire Eternal ruling #1, Shivan Meteor ruling #11]. Note that "without paying its mana cost" also means Amelia couldn't substitute an alternative cost even if one existed [Shivan Meteor ruling #6]. If Amelia wants to suspend Shivan Meteor for {1}{R}{R} instead, she must do it at a time she holds priority — for example, before the trigger goes on the stack or after it finishes resolving, at any point she could begin casting Shivan Meteor from hand [116.2f, 702.62a, Shivan Meteor ruling #12]. Since Shivan Meteor is a sorcery, that means a main phase of her own turn with an empty stack, not during combat.

This answer is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents (Wildfire Eternal's afflict and "attacks and isn't blocked" ability only care about the one defending player it's attacking).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold:
Yes. The suspend special action can be taken whenever Shivan Meteor could be cast from Amelia's hand. Normally that's only when Amelia has priority on their turn with an empty stack, but in this case the effect of Wildfire Eternal is letting that happen while the ability resolves.

(They still have to pay the suspend cost, and afterwards they can choose to cast a different spell from hand without paying its mana cost.)

question: Asa controls [Library of Leng] and is discarding a card due to [Azra Oddsmaker]'s ability. Can they put the discarded card on top of their library? If so, what happens?
answer:
No — Asa must put the discarded card into their graveyard. Library of Leng doesn't apply to Azra Oddsmaker's discard, because that discard is a cost, not an effect.

Why: Azra Oddsmaker's triggered ability reads "you may discard a card. If you do, choose a creature..." That's exactly the template covered by rule 118.12 — "[A player] may [do something]. If [that player] [does]..." — and that rule states the "[do something]" action is a cost, paid as the triggered ability resolves. Library of Leng's replacement only works "If an effect causes you to discard a card," and its ruling is explicit that you can't use it when you discard as a cost, because costs aren't effects (rule 609.1 confirms an effect is something produced by a resolving spell/ability or a static ability, and text itself is never an effect) [Library of Leng ruling #5].

What does happen: if Asa chooses to discard, the card goes from hand to graveyard, Asa has paid the cost, and Azra Oddsmaker's ability continues — Asa chooses a creature, and whenever that creature deals combat damage to a player this turn, Asa draws two cards. Note that under rule 118.12 the "If you do" clause checks whether the player started to pay the cost, so even if some other effect altered what actually happened during the discard, the cost would still count as paid (compare rule 118.11). Library of Leng's other ability — Asa has no maximum hand size — is unaffected and still applies.

If instead the discard came from an effect that just tells you to discard (e.g., a resolving spell's instruction, not an "If you do" cost), Library of Leng would let Asa put that card on top of their library instead, and it would still count as a discard for anything that triggers on discarding [Library of Leng ruling #4].

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so it works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Yes. Discarding a cost to the ability is a cost [118.12], but that doesn't stop it from being an effect as well. Library of Leng only changes where the card moves to, not that it was discarded, so the cost was paid and the remainder of Azra Oddsmaker's ability will resolve as normal.

question: Nixon has a [Southern Elephant] and a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters in their graveyard. Addison casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nixon. What happens to the counters on the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave? Will Nixon know which manifested card is which?
answer:
Short answer: the three +1/+1 counters stay on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave the whole way, so it arrives as a face-down manifested permanent that is a 2/2 with three +1/+1 counters on it — a 5/5. Because Southern Elephant will manifest as a plain 2/2, everyone at the table (including Nixon) can tell which face-down permanent is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave, even though the pile was shuffled.

Why the counters survive:
- Normally counters on an object cease to exist when it changes zones ([122.2]), but Skullbriar, the Walking Grave's own text says "Counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player's hand or library." Card text beats the general rule here.
- Ghastly Conscription moves the cards graveyard → exile → battlefield. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has its abilities in the graveyard, so the counters remain when it's exiled, and it still has its abilities as a card in the face-down exile pile (being exiled face down only limits who may examine it — [406.3]), so the counters remain again when it's manifested onto the battlefield. That the ability must be present in the zone the card is leaving is exactly what [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2] describes.
- Those counters aren't "placed" on it, so counter-doubling or counter-hosing effects don't interact with them ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1]), and it retains counters of every kind, not just +1/+1 ([Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #6]).

What the manifested permanent is: manifesting turns the card face down and puts it onto the battlefield as a 2/2 face-down creature with no name, no text, no subtypes, and no mana cost ([701.40a], [708.2], [708.2a], [Ghastly Conscription ruling #9]). Face down, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave has no abilities and is not legendary — but the three counters are on the permanent independently of its characteristics, making it 5/5. Southern Elephant manifests as an ordinary 2/2.

So, does Nixon know which is which? Yes, in practice. The shuffle is meant to hide which manifested card is which ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #4]), and Nixon may not look at face-down permanents they don't control ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #14]) — Addison cast Ghastly Conscription, so Addison manifests and controls both permanents and may look at them. But the visible +1/+1 counters give it away: the 5/5 is Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and the 2/2 is Southern Elephant. Note also that Addison is the one who could turn either face up by paying its mana cost as a special action — {B}{G} for Skullbriar, the Walking Grave or {3}{G} for Southern Elephant ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #3]).

Player count: nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table; Ghastly Conscription targets one player's graveyard either way. One multiplayer wrinkle from the card's own rulings: if Addison manifests a card owned by Nixon and Addison later leaves the game, that card is exiled ([Ghastly Conscription ruling #7]).

Timing note: I'm assuming the counters were already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave in the graveyard before Ghastly Conscription resolved. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave somehow had no counters at the moment Ghastly Conscription resolved, both manifested permanents would be indistinguishable 2/2s and Nixon would not know which is which.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: When in the graveyard, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had the ability that allowed it to keep its counters, so it is exiled and shuffled with 3 +1/+1 counters. When it's moved to the battlefield, it's face down and no longer has that ability, so the counters cease to exist. It had the counters immediately before entering the battlefield however, so Nixon will know which face-down permanent is the Skullbriar, the Walking Grave and which is the Southern Elephant.

question: Abdullah controls [Primal Vigor] and casts [Rescuer Sphinx], choosing to return Primal Vigor to their hand. How many +1/+1 counters will Rescuer Sphinx enter the battlefield with?
answer:
Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield with just one +1/+1 counter, not two.

Why: Rescuer Sphinx's ability ("As this creature enters, you may return a nonland permanent you control to its owner's hand. If you do, this creature enters with a +1/+1 counter on it") is a replacement effect that modifies how Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield [614.1c], and such an effect may cause another object to change zones as part of applying it [614.13a]. The choice is made and carried out before Rescuer Sphinx is actually on the battlefield, and no player may take actions in between [Rescuer Sphinx ruling #3].

So the sequence is: Abdullah applies Rescuer Sphinx's replacement effect, returning Primal Vigor from the battlefield to his hand, and only then is it established that Rescuer Sphinx enters with a +1/+1 counter. Primal Vigor's doubling ability is a static ability that functions only while Primal Vigor is on the battlefield; once it has been returned to hand it is no longer an existing continuous effect that could apply. When you determine which replacement effects apply to a permanent entering the battlefield, you look at the replacement effects that have already modified how it enters plus the continuous effects that already exist and would apply to it [614.12], [614.12a], [616.1]. At that moment Primal Vigor's effect no longer exists, so nothing doubles the counter.

Note also that Primal Vigor's second ability can't be applied "first": it only applies if one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on a creature [614.16], and until Rescuer Sphinx's own replacement effect is applied (including the return), the number of counters Rescuer Sphinx would enter with is zero. The replaced event simply never happens in the un-doubled-then-doubled way — the modified event is what occurs [614.6].

If instead Abdullah returned some other nonland permanent (or returned nothing but had another way to get the counter), Primal Vigor would still be on the battlefield and would double the counter — Rescuer Sphinx would enter with two +1/+1 counters, since Primal Vigor explicitly affects permanents that enter with counters [Primal Vigor ruling #3], and it doesn't matter who controls the creature getting the counters [Primal Vigor ruling #2].

Player count doesn't change any of this: the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table. The only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that if several players must order overlapping replacement effects at the same time, those choices are made in APNAP order [616.1] — which doesn't come up here, since Abdullah controls Rescuer Sphinx and makes all the relevant choices himself.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Two. Both cards have a replacement effect. Abdullah will choose whether they are returning a permanent, but won't actually complete the action until Rescuer Sphinx enters the battlefield. Therefore Primal Vigor will still apply to the +1/+1 counter being from Rescuer Sphinx's ability.

question: Aryana controls [Ascended Lawmage] and [Cemetery Gate]. Nicholas controls [Onakke Ogre] enchanted by their [Paralyze]. Aryana casts [Sudden Disappearance] targeting Nicholas. When the trigger resolves at the beginning of the next end step, what can Paralyze enchant?
answer:
Nicholas chooses, and his legal choices are Onakke Ogre (which returns to the battlefield at the same time) or Aryana's Ascended Lawmage — but not Aryana's Cemetery Gate.

Why:

- Sudden Disappearance exiled every nonland permanent Nicholas controlled, which includes both Onakke Ogre and Paralyze itself (an Aura is a nonland permanent). At the beginning of the next end step the delayed trigger returns those cards to the battlefield under their owner's control, so Paralyze comes back under Nicholas's control.
- Because Paralyze is entering the battlefield by something other than resolving as an Aura spell, and Sudden Disappearance doesn't specify what it enchants, Nicholas chooses what Paralyze enchants as it enters, and the choice must be legal for its enchant creature ability and any other applicable effects [303.4f]. This is not targeting.
- Ascended Lawmage is a legal choice. Hexproof only stops it from being the target of spells or abilities its controller's opponents control [702.11b]; attaching an Aura on entry involves no targeting, so hexproof doesn't prevent Nicholas from choosing Ascended Lawmage. Paralyze's enters trigger would then tap Ascended Lawmage, and it wouldn't untap during Aryana's untap step unless Aryana pays {4} at the beginning of her upkeep.
- Cemetery Gate is not a legal choice. Paralyze is a black Aura (mana cost {B}), and a permanent with protection from black can't be enchanted by black Auras; if one somehow ended up attached, it would go to its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [702.16c]. So Nicholas can't choose Cemetery Gate under rule 303.4f's "legal object" requirement.
- Onakke Ogre returns to the battlefield simultaneously with Paralyze, and it's an ordinary creature with no protection or other restriction, so it's the natural (and typical) choice. Note the provided rules don't include a specific rule text about attaching to permanents entering simultaneously; if your group rules that only creatures already on the battlefield count, Nicholas's only remaining option in the two-player setup described would be Ascended Lawmage.
- Any other creature on the battlefield is also a legal choice if it has no protection/other restriction. If Paralyze has no legal object to enchant at all, it can't enter attached to anything.

Multiplayer: the analysis is unchanged in substance. Sudden Disappearance targets a single player (Nicholas), so only his nonland permanents were exiled; with more than two players, Nicholas may also choose any legal creature controlled by any other player at the table, subject to the same protection restriction [702.16c] and the legality requirement of [303.4f].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Just Ascended Lawmage. Cemetery Gate has protection from black, so it can't be enchanted by anything black. Onakke Ogre isn't on the battlefield when Nicholas chooses what to enchant. Hexproof doesn't prevent an Aura from becoming attached to the Ascended Lawmage.

question: Albert, Brielle, and Campbell are playing a multiplayer game. Brielle controls [Stalking Leonin]. Albert casts [Worst Fears] to take control of Brielle's next turn. After Brielle begins their turn, can Albert see which player was chosen for the Stalking Leonin?
answer:
Yes. Once Brielle's turn begins and Albert is controlling Brielle, Albert can see which opponent was secretly chosen for Brielle's Stalking Leonin.

Why: Stalking Leonin's enters-the-battlefield trigger has Brielle "secretly choose an opponent," and that choice is recorded somehow (for example, by writing the player's name on a slip of paper kept with Stalking Leonin) — it is hidden information about Stalking Leonin, an object in the game, that Brielle knows. Rule 723.4 says that if information about an object in the game would be visible to the player being controlled, it's visible to both that player and the controller of that player. So Albert, as the controller of Brielle, sees it. Worst Fears' own reminder text says the same thing in short form — "You see all cards that player could see and make all decisions for them" — and its rulings confirm that while controlling another player you can see all cards in the game that player can see, including cards in hand and face-down cards that player controls.

Two limits worth noting. First, this only extends to in-game information: rule 723.4 specifies that information about cards outside the game (such as a sideboard) that would be visible to Brielle is visible only to Brielle, not to Albert. The Stalking Leonin choice is in-game information, so it isn't covered by that exception. Second, Albert controls Brielle, not Brielle's permanents — per Worst Fears' rulings, Albert only controls the player and doesn't control any of Brielle's permanents, spells, or abilities. Albert still makes Brielle's decisions, so Albert could decide to activate Stalking Leonin's last ability, paying its cost by revealing the chosen player — but that ability needs a legal target, a creature attacking Brielle controlled by the chosen player, and during Brielle's own turn Brielle is the active player, so there generally won't be creatures attacking Brielle to target.

This answer is for the three-player game as described (Albert, Brielle, Campbell); rule 723.4 works the same regardless of the number of players, and Campbell's presence doesn't change it. Campbell does not gain any right to see the secret choice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: No. The choice was made as Stalking Leonin entered the battlefield, which already happened- it's no longer visible to Brielle. Albert can choose to activate the ability (at which point all players will know who was chosen), but otherwise the choice is not visible to any player.

question: At the beginning of the game, Alianna announced [Zirda, the Dawnwaker] as their companion. During the game, Alianna cast [Glistening Goremonger] from their sideboard with [Wish]. Later, Alianna restarts the game with [Karn Liberated]. What happens?
answer:
Short answer: the game restarts, and Alianna's Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger card — which came in from outside the game via Wish — is shuffled into Alianna's library for the new game. During the new game's pregame procedure Alianna may reveal Zirda, the Dawnwaker as their companion again, and the condition is still met, because Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger is a permanent card that has an activated ability ({3}{B/P}: Transform this creature).

Details:

1. Restarting. Karn Liberated's −14 immediately ends the current game with no winner, loser, or drawer, and the same players begin a new game using the normal starting procedure of rule 103, with the exception in rule 727.2 [727.1] [727.2] [Karn Liberated]. Non-Aura permanent cards exiled with Karn Liberated stay in exile and enter the battlefield under Alianna's control after the pregame procedure finishes [Karn Liberated].

2. The Wished card. Rule 727.2 says every Magic card involved in the ended game is involved in the new game, even if it wasn't originally part of it — its example is exactly a creature card brought in from outside the game with a Wish-style effect, which becomes part of that player's library in the new game [727.2] [Wish]. So Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger is now one of Alianna's deck cards; it can't be shuffled back into the sideboard, since players can't move cards between deck and sideboard before the new game [Karn Liberated]. (Pedantic note: Glistening Goremonger is the back face; what Alianna actually cast with Wish was the front face, Pyretic Prankster.)

3. Companion in the new game. Companion is a keyword that functions from outside the game: before the game begins you may reveal one card you own from outside the game whose companion condition is satisfied by your starting deck, and once during the game you may pay {3} as a special action to put it into your hand [702.139a] [103.2b]. Because a restart runs the full starting procedure, the companion-reveal step happens again [727.1] [103.2b], and the "once during the game" {3} special action is fresh for the new game [702.139a].

4. Is Zirda, the Dawnwaker still legal? Zirda, the Dawnwaker requires that each permanent card in your starting deck have an activated ability [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. Pyretic Prankster // Glistening Goremonger is a creature (permanent) card, and it has the activated ability "{3}{B/P}: Transform this creature. Activate only as a sorcery." — activated abilities are the ones written "[Cost]: [Effect]" [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. So adding it to the deck does not break the condition, and Alianna may reveal Zirda, the Dawnwaker again. Zirda, the Dawnwaker itself was never brought into the game (it stayed outside the game as a revealed companion), so it is available to be revealed once more.

5. Timing assumption. I'm assuming Alianna never paid the {3} to put Zirda, the Dawnwaker into their hand before the restart. If Alianna had already paid {3} and Zirda, the Dawnwaker was in hand (or graveyard, battlefield, etc.) when the game restarted, then Zirda, the Dawnwaker would be a card "involved in the game" and would be shuffled into Alianna's library for the new game [727.2], and a card sitting in your starting deck can't function as your companion — the companion ability has no effect from inside the deck [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. Alianna would then have no companion in the new game.

6. Two players vs. multiplayer. With more than two players, the controller of the restarting ability (Alianna) is the starting player in the new game, any player who had already left the game before the restart is not in the new game [Karn Liberated], and companions are revealed starting with the starting player and proceeding in turn order — once a player declines, they can't change their mind [103.2b] [Zirda, the Dawnwaker]. In a two-player game that just means Alianna declares first. Nothing else about this interaction differs by player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Glistening Goremonger will be shuffled into Alianna's library along with the rest of the cards in the game. Because Glistening Goremonger violates Zirda, the Dawnwaker's companion restriction, Alianna can't announce it as their companion for the restarted game.

question: Allyson controls [Ice Cauldron]. Nico controls [Suppression Field]. Allyson activates Ice Cauldron's first ability with X=1, paying {C}{C}{C}. On Allyson's next turn, they activate Ice Cauldron's second ability. How much mana do they add?
answer:
Allyson adds {C}{C}{C} — three colorless mana.

Why: Ice Cauldron's first ability reads "{X}, {T}: ... note the type and amount of mana spent to pay this activation cost." Suppression Field says "Activated abilities cost {2} more to activate unless they're mana abilities," and Ice Cauldron's first ability is an activated ability that produces no mana, so the {2} increase applies. Ice Cauldron's activation cost is its analog to a spell's mana cost, and the total cost is that cost plus all cost increases, locked in once determined ([602.1a], [602.2b], [601.2f]). With X=1 that total is {1} + {2} = {3} generic (plus tapping Ice Cauldron), which Allyson paid with {C}{C}{C}.

Ice Cauldron notes the actual mana spent, not the value of X — the ruling that it "counts only mana spent on it. It doesn't see the value of X, so isn't affected by cost reductions" cuts the same way for cost increases. So it noted {C}{C}{C}, and the second ability adds exactly that: {C}{C}{C}. Note that {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic; it can pay generic costs but nothing that demands a color.

Two other points:
- Ice Cauldron's second ability is a mana ability (per its ruling, "Tapping the Cauldron for the mana is a mana ability"), so Suppression Field does not add {2} to activating it. Its cost stays {T} plus removing a charge counter.
- That {C}{C}{C} can only be spent to cast the last card exiled with Ice Cauldron, though Allyson may add other mana from elsewhere to finish paying that spell's cost, including additional costs.

This is the same whether the game has two players or more — Suppression Field affects every player's non-mana activated abilities, including its controller Nico's, so the number of opponents doesn't change the result.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
answer_gold: Just {C}. The activation cost of Ice Cauldron's first ability is "{X}, {T}". The additional cost imposed by Suppression Field is not part of the activation cost, and the mana spent on it isn't noted when the ability resolves.
